messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Counselor
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Avoid People: avoid other people, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Sudden Pieces: Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Robert's Reckoning

Robert Chen had always understood himself as a man who sat with other people's pain. At sixty-eight, he had spent forty-two years as a school counselor, the steady presence in the office down the hall where teenagers came to talk about their parents' divorces, their academic failures, their first heartbreaks. He had built a reputation for genuine warmth, for the kind of listening that made kids feel seen. His wife, Maria, used to joke that he had given away all his emotional reserves at work, leaving her only the tired version at home. She had said it without real bitterness, the way couples do when they have negotiated the same small resentment for decades. Robert had laughed along, though something in him had always known it was true.

The assault happened on a Tuesday evening in March, eight months before he came to seek help. Robert had stayed late at Lincoln High to help a student through a crisis—a junior named DeShawn whose mother had been hospitalized. Robert had driven the boy home, waited while he got inside safely, and was leaving the neighborhood when a man stepped out from between two parked cars. Robert remembered the smell first: stale alcohol and something chemical, like cheap cologne mixed with sweat. The man had a knife. What followed was a blur of movement and terror, Robert's body responding in ways he could not control, his voice gone, his hands up. The man took his wallet, his watch, and something else—something Robert could not quite name but felt stolen nonetheless. When the police found him twenty minutes later, sitting on a curb three blocks away, Robert was still shaking so hard he could barely give his name.

The physical injuries healed within weeks. But something else had fractured, and Robert found himself unable to piece it back together. The first time he smelled the antiseptic scent of the hospital during his follow-up appointment, his body had seized as if the knife were coming again. His heart had raced. His vision had narrowed. He had sat in the waiting room sweating, certain he was dying, until a nurse led him to a back office and closed the door. After that, he could not enter a hospital without that same cascading panic, so he stopped going. His regular physical—overdue by a year—went unscheduled.

Within weeks, the hospital smell began to find him elsewhere. The cleaning supplies used by the custodians at Lincoln High smelled vaguely similar. Robert started timing his arrival and departure to avoid passing the supply closet. Then he began eating lunch in his car instead of the faculty lounge. Then he stopped attending staff meetings, claiming administrative work that required him to stay in his office. His principal, concerned, had asked if everything was all right. Robert had said yes, just managing some personal matters. The lie had felt necessary.

But the worst part was not the smells. It was the memory itself, which had begun to ambush him without warning. A fragment would surface—the man's face, the smell, the particular angle of the knife in the streetlight—and Robert would be back there, the terror identical to that Tuesday evening, flooding through him as if no time had passed at all. These moments lasted only seconds, but they left him shaken for hours afterward. He had learned to dissociate deliberately when he felt one coming, to mentally leave his body, to blank himself out. It was the only thing that worked. He would sit at his desk, seemingly present, while his mind retreated somewhere far away where the memory could not touch him.

Maria had noticed the distance first. She had tried to hold his hand while watching television, and he had pulled away without thinking. When she had asked what was wrong, he had said nothing, he was just tired. But the truth was that her closeness terrified him in a way he could not articulate. The idea of being emotionally intimate, of letting her see inside him, felt like an unbearable vulnerability. He had begun sleeping in the guest room, telling her his snoring had gotten worse. He stopped going to their friends' dinner parties. He avoided his adult children's phone calls. The isolation had become total, a protective shell he did not know how to break.

It was Maria who finally insisted he see someone. She had found him one morning unable to get out of bed, not from depression exactly but from a kind of paralysis, a fear so diffuse he could not name its object. "This is not living," she had said quietly. "I don't know what happened to you that night, but I know you're still there, and I want my husband back." Robert had sat across from her at the kitchen table, feeling the weight of forty-five years of marriage, and had finally said the words aloud: "I was attacked. I can't stop being afraid." Now, sitting in the therapist's office, he was terrified that the fear was permanent, that he had already lost too much time, and that the man he had been—the counselor, the listener, the husband—was gone for good.
